title: Conditional or Joint?
short: P(A ∩ B) is the chance that both happen; P(A ∣ B) is the chance of A among the outcomes where B happens. Read the question to see which one it asks for.
trouble: Students answer with the joint probability P(A ∩ B) when the question asks "of those with B, what fraction have A?", or divide by the wrong event.

blocks.html: Two probabilities are easy to mix up: the chance that A and B both happen, and the chance of A among the cases where B happens. You met both in the general multiplication rule, $P(A \cap B) = P(B)\,P(A \mid B)$. Most wrong answers in conditioning problems are right answers to the other question, so this lesson is about reading the question.

$P(A \cap B)$, the joint probability, is a share of everything. $P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, the conditional probability, is a share of B. Words like "of those who", "among", "given" and "if" name the group to divide by; "both" or "and" with no such phrase asks for the joint.

Knowing that B happened rules out every outcome outside B, so B becomes the new sample space. To keep the total at 1, every probability inside B is rescaled by $\frac{1}{P(B)}$. The part of A that survives is $A \cap B$, so its new probability is $\frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$. The function $A \mapsto P(A \mid B)$ satisfies all three axioms, so conditional probabilities obey every rule you know: complements, the addition rule, and so on.

blocks.name: prob-square
blocks.cap: The joint probability is the overlap as a share of the whole square. Conditioning on Late stretches the Late region to fill the square, and the share that Rain covers there is the conditional probability.

blocks.html: In the picture, the overlap has area $\frac{1}{5}$ of the square: that is $P(\text{Rain} \cap \text{Late})$. Inside the Late region (area $\frac{2}{5}$) it covers half: that is $P(\text{Rain} \mid \text{Late}) = \frac{1/5}{2/5} = \frac{1}{2}$. Same overlap, two different denominators.

blocks.title: One table, three questions
blocks.q: Of 200 students, 60 play a sport; 24 of those also have a part-time job; 56 students have a job in all. A student is picked at random. Find (a) the fraction who play a sport and have a job, (b) of the athletes, the fraction with a job, (c) of those with a job, the fraction who play a sport.
steps: (a) No group is named, and "and" asks for both: $P(S \cap J) = \frac{24}{200} = \frac{3}{25}$.
(b) "Of the athletes" divides by the 60 athletes: $P(J \mid S) = \frac{24}{60} = \frac{2}{5}$.
(c) "Of those with a job" divides by the 56 workers: $P(S \mid J) = \frac{24}{56} = \frac{3}{7}$.
blocks.a: $\frac{3}{25}$, $\frac{2}{5}$ and $\frac{3}{7}$: the same 24 students, three different denominators.

blocks.title: From percents
blocks.q: Of a café's customers, 40% buy coffee and 15% buy both coffee and a pastry. Of the coffee buyers, what fraction buy a pastry?
steps: The 15% is joint: a share of all customers. The question names the coffee buyers as the group.

blocks.title: Going the other way
blocks.q: 60% of a library's visitors are adults, and 25% of the adults borrow a DVD. What fraction of all visitors are adults who borrow a DVD?
steps: 25% is conditional (a share of the adults); the question asks for a share of everyone, a joint probability.

blocks.html: Answering "of those with B, what fraction have A?" with the joint $P(A \cap B)$, or dividing by the wrong event and giving $P(B \mid A)$ instead of $P(A \mid B)$. Check: name the group the question restricts to, and make sure it is your denominator. A conditional probability is never smaller than the joint one, since $P(B) \le 1$.
